id: A Note Left in Jimmy Leonard’s Shack

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Near the dry river’s water-mark we found Your brother Minnegan, Flopped like a fish against the muddy ground. Beany, the kid whose yellow hair turns green, Told me to find you, even in the rain, And tell you he was drowned. I hid behind the chassis on the bank, The wreck of someone’s Ford: I was afraid to come and wake you drunk: You told me once the waking up was hard, The daylight beating at you like a board. Blood in my stomach sank. Beside, you told him never to go out Along the river-side Drinking and singing, clattering about. You might have thrown a rock at me and cried I was to blame, I let him fall in the road And pitch down on his side. Well, I’ll get hell enough when I get home For coming up this far, Leaving the note, and running as I came. I’ll go and tell my father where you are. You’d better go find Minnegan before Policemen hear and come. Beany went home, and I got sick and ran, You old son of a bitch. You better hurry down to Minnegan; He’s drunk or dying now, I don’t know which, Rolled in the roots and garbage like a fish, The poor old man.

Here are two ways to polish the text, depending on the tone you wish to achieve:

### Option 1: Eloquent & Literary Narrative
*This version elevates the poetic storytelling into articulate, expressive prose while retaining all emotional tension, sensory details, and original narrative points.*

> We discovered your brother, Minnegan, lying prone on the muddy earth near the dry river's high-water mark, flailing helplessly like a stranded fish. Beany—the boy whose yellow hair shifts to green in the water—urged me to brave the rain, locate you, and report that your brother had drowned.
> 
> Terrified of disturbing you in your drunken state, I concealed myself behind the rusted chassis of an old Ford abandoned on the embankment. I remembered your past warning of how agonizing it is to awaken—how the harsh daylight strikes you like a wooden beam—and dread sank deep into my stomach. Furthermore, you had explicitly forbidden him from wandering along the riverbank while drinking, singing, and causing a commotion. I feared that in your rage, you might hurl a stone at me and accuse me of allowing him to stumble and fall along the road.
> 
> I will undoubtedly face severe consequences at home for venturing this far, leaving behind a hasty note, and fleeing. I intend to inform my father of your current whereabouts, but you must make haste to find Minnegan before the authorities are alerted. Beany has already returned home, and overwhelmed by sudden illness, I too turned and fled. 
> 
> You miserable, stubborn man—you must hurry down to Minnegan at once. Whether he is merely insensible from liquor or at death's door, I cannot tell. The poor old man lies there, entangled in exposed roots and river debris like a landed fish.

---

### Option 2: Formal & Structured Statement
*If "professional" requires a clear, objective incident report while preserving every detail from the original text.*

> **Subject:** Urgent Notice Regarding Minnegan
> 
> Your brother, Minnegan, was located near the dry river’s high-water mark, lying collapsed on the muddy ground like a stranded fish. Beany (the boy with yellow hair that turns green) instructed me to brave the rain to find you and report that your brother appears to have drowned. 
> 
> Upon arrival, I hid behind the chassis of an abandoned Ford on the riverbank. I was afraid to wake you in your intoxicated state, recalling your description of how painful it is to awaken hungover, with the daylight striking you like a board. The situation caused a sickening sense of dread in my stomach. Additionally, I recalled your warnings to Minnegan never to go out along the riverbank drinking, singing, and making noise. I feared you might react aggressively—perhaps throwing a stone at me—and blame me for letting him fall on the road.
> 
> I expect to face serious trouble at home for traveling this far, leaving a note, and running back. I am going to inform my father of your location. However, you must go find Minnegan immediately, before the police are alerted. Beany has returned home, and I felt sick and ran away. 
> 
> You need to hurry to Minnegan immediately. It is unclear whether he is unconscious from alcohol or currently dying. The poor old man is collapsed among the riverbank roots and garbage like a fish.
outputs.L2:
We discovered your sibling, Minnegan, lying on the wet earth close to the high-water line of the dry creek bed, twisting around like a landed aquatic creature. The fair-haired boy named Beany—the one whose blonde locks take on a greenish hue—urged me to brave the downpour to locate you and report that your brother had perished in the water. 

Overcome with dread, my stomach churned, so I concealed myself near the embankment behind the stripped frame of an abandoned Ford automobile. I was hesitant to rouse you from your drunken stupor, remembering how you once described the agonizing pain of a hangover, as if the morning light were physically striking you like a wooden beam. Furthermore, I recalled that you had forbidden Minnegan from ever wandering near the shoreline while drinking, singing, and making a racket. I worried you would lash out, hurl a rock at me, and falsely accuse me of letting him stumble and fall onto the path. 

I am going to face severe punishment at home for traveling this far, dropping off this note, and sprinting back. I plan to inform my father of your current location. You need to retrieve Minnegan immediately before law enforcement gets wind of this and arrives at the scene. 

While Beany headed back to his house, I was overwhelmed by nausea and ran, you miserable bastard. Hurry down to Minnegan right away; I cannot tell if he is merely severely intoxicated or in his final moments, tangled in the litter and tree roots like a fish out of water—that unfortunate elderly man.
outputs.L3:
I stood in the doorway, my boots still caked with wet river clay, staring at your slouched form in the armchair. The room reeked of stale whiskey and sweat. You were out cold, snoring heavily, an empty bottle lying on its side near your foot. I reached out a hand to shake you awake, but stopped myself, my fingers hovering in the air. I knew better than to wake you when you were like this. When the liquor took hold of you, a sudden startle usually meant a heavy fist swung out before your eyes even opened. 

Just twenty minutes ago, I was down by the lower bend when one of the neighborhood kids came running up to me, gasping for breath, shouting that your brother Minnegan had drowned. I ran as fast as my legs would carry me down to the water’s edge. He wasn't dead, thank God, but it was close. I found Minnegan collapsed face-down in the thick, icy mud near the riverbank, barely moving, the rising tide licking at his boots. 

It was exactly what you had warned him about. I lost count of how many times I heard you yell at the old man, telling him to stay away from the riverside, especially when he’d been drinking. But Minnegan was stubborn, and tonight, his wandering almost cost him his life.

I stepped back from your chair, my heart pounding in my chest. Panic started to set in. It was way past the time I was supposed to be home, and my parents would skin me alive if they caught me out this late. Worse than that, I knew how your mind worked. If I stayed here and woke you up, you’d find a way to make this my fault. You’d accuse me of pushing him, or playing a trick, or leaving the old man out there to rot. I couldn't bear the brunt of your temper—not tonight.

Fearing your wrath and the belt waiting for me at home, I decided I couldn't stay. 

I scrambled around the messy kitchen until I found a stubby pencil and an old paper grocery bag. With trembling hands, I scribbled a message in frantic, jagged letters, flattening the scrap against the wooden table. 

I pinned the note to the table right beside your elbow with a kitchen knife so you wouldn't miss it, took one last look at your sleeping frame, and slipped out into the dark, fleeing into the night. 

***

*The Note Reads:*

> **WAKE UP!** 
> 
> Minnegan is down at the riverbank near the lower bend. He’s collapsed in the mud and can’t get up. I know you told him to stay away from the water when he's been drinking, but he didn't listen. 
> 
> You need to hurry down there right now and haul the old man out before the tide comes up any higher—or before the police find him and lock him away. 
> 
> Move fast!
outputs.L4:
The door creaked open, releasing a stale cloud of cheap whiskey and damp wool into the cold night air. I hovered on the threshold, my boots coated in thick, riverbed clay, my heart hammering a frantic rhythm against my ribs. Inside, slouched in a sagging armchair beside a dying fire, sat the man I feared almost as much as the dark. His shoulders were broad, heavy with a lifetime of hard labor and bad liquor, and even in his drunken stupor, he radiated a volatile, simmering menace. I kept my hand near the doorframe, ready to bolt at the first sign of a swing.

"Thomas," I whispered, my voice trembling despite my best efforts to keep it steady. "Thomas, wake up. Please."

He grunted, a low, guttural sound, and shifted his heavy head. Bleary, bloodshot eyes fixed on me through the dim light of the lantern. I saw the sudden spark of irritability flare in his brow—the dangerous, unpredictable spark that usually presaged a broken chair or a bruised jaw. I took a half-step back, speaking as quickly and softly as my fluttering lungs would allow, desperate to drop the words between us before his temper could detonate.

"It’s Minnegan," I blurted, clutching the edge of the door. "I found him down by the low bank, near the old mill outlet. You got to come."

Thomas blinked, the fog of alcohol delaying the meaning of my words. He reached for the half-empty bottle on the floor beside him, his massive hand wrapping around the neck like a club. "What’s that fool done now?" he rumbled, his voice thick and slurred. "If he’s sleeping off another bender, let him rot."

"He *can't* move, Thomas," I pressed, the terror for the boy down by the water briefly eclipsing my fear of the man in front of me. "He’s wedged down in the mud, half-submerged. He’s rolled right up in the gnarled roots and the river garbage—tangled in rotted driftwood and plastic scrap. I couldn't drag him free on my own."

I paused, swallowing hard, remembering the ghastly sight. Minnegan’s face had been slick with black mud, his mouth open to the drizzling sky. 

"I couldn't tell if he was breathing, Thomas," I added, my voice cracking. "He’s either dead-drunk or just... plain dying. He’s cold as river stone."

For a long, agonizing second, Thomas just stared at me. The silence in the cabin grew suffocating, thick with the smell of spilled spirits and impending violence. I tensed my legs, waiting for him to leap up in a rage, to blame me for his brother’s ruin. 

Instead, I played my last, most urgent card. 

"And Thomas... I saw headlamps crawling down the ridge road," I hissed, leaning forward just an inch. "The county patrol. They’re searching the lower tracks. If they find Minnegan down there like that, wrapped up in the mire... you know what they’ll do. They’ll haul him off, or worse. You have to get him now, before they reach the bank."

The mention of the law hit Thomas like a bucket of ice water. The dim lethargy in his eyes snapped into sudden, sharp focus. The threat of the police—and the certainty of a tragedy if they found Minnegan first—seemed to burn right through the whiskey fog. 

Slowly, heavily, Thomas stood up. The bottle clattered to the floorboards, rolling away ignored. He didn't strike out, nor did he yell. He simply grabbed his heavy oilskin coat from the peg on the wall, his breathing ragged and deep, and shoved past me into the dark, wet night. I fell in behind him, leading the way back down toward the river, terrified of what we might find waiting for us in the mud.

Tucked just beyond the rush of the main highway, hidden behind a canopy of ancient oaks, lies a place that time seems to have forgotten. If you travel down the winding country road **near your** hometown, you might just stumble upon the quiet, sun-dappled valley of **Minnegan**.

**Minnegan** isn’t the kind of place you find on a flashy tourist map. It is a peaceful sanctuary of red-brick storefronts, rustling birch trees, and morning air so crisp it clears **your** mind the moment you step outside. Local legend says the town was founded by travelers who simply stopped to rest by the stream, looked around, and realized they had already reached their destination.

As evening falls and a soft mist settles **near** the riverbanks, warm yellow light pours from the windows of the local cafes. It is remarkably easy to lose track of time here. Whether you are walking along the old cobblestone paths or sitting on a wooden porch watching the stars, **Minnegan** offers a rare gift: the chance to slow down, breathe deeply, and reconnect with what truly matters to **your** heart.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a gritty narrative poem from the perspective of a young boy delivering tragic news to a volatile, alcoholic man about his brother Minnegan, who has fallen into the muddy riverbank.
counterfactuals.output:
I held my breath before I kicked the rotting pine;
The porch was slick with sleet, the hinges hissed like grease.
I stepped into the dark, into the stink of sour mash,
Where shadows chewed the corners of a broken lease.

He sat behind the lamp, a monument of threat,
A brown bottle clutched like a club within his fist.
His breath was heat and rye, his knuckles split and raw,
His eyes two bloody cinders burning through the mist.

"Speak up, you little rat, before I break your skin,"
He growled it low and heavy, like a kettle at the boil.
I backed against the doorframe, cap squeezed in my palms,
My small knees shaking under rain and river soil.

"It’s Minnegan," I choked. The name fell on the floor.
He didn't raise his head, but I could hear his teeth click shut.
The room grew tight as wire, the air turned thin and cold,
And I could smell the thunder rising from his gut.

"Down past the tallow plant," I sobbed, and took a step,
"Where the clay caves in and the bank is black and steep...
Minnegan slipped the ridge—he tried to catch the weed—
But the river mud was heavy, and the trench was deep."

He shifted in his chair. The wood began to groan.
I pressed my spine to pine and forced the rest on out:
"The silt came up like paste and pulled him by the boots;
He hollered for you once, a awful, strangled shout.

I tried to reach his sleeve—I swear to God I tried!
I laid flat on the timber, but the current dragged him clear.
The brown mud swallowed up his chin, and then his mouth...
He’s down beneath the pylons, mister. Underneath the pier."

The silence in the shack was louder than the rain.
He didn't swing a fist. He didn't curse or cry.
He only raised the bottle, drained the amber dark,
And stared right through my face with a flat and yellow eye.

Then slow, like shifting stone, he stood and dropped the glass.
It shattered on the floorboards, soaking in his shoes.
He pushed past through the doorway, out into the night,
Leaving me alone with the mud, and him, and news.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dramatic monologue in verse reminiscent of Robert Frost or James Wright. It should feature a child hiding behind a wrecked Ford chassis, afraid to wake an angry drunk to tell him his brother has drowned.
counterfactuals.output:
The iron leaf-spring bites into my knee,
But I don’t move. I keep my forehead pressed
Against the flaking oxide of the door—
A thirty-nine, he said, before the weeds
Grew through the floorboard and the steering wheel.

Across the dirt, the screen door hangs unlatched.
I see his boots. He’s sleeping on the porch,
Slumped in the wicker rocker with the jar
Tipped empty at his heel. His breathing comes
In heavy, sour rasps—like pulling wet
Burlap across a floor. If I step out,
The gravel screams. The dark will catch my shape.

I ought to run and shake him by the shirt.
I ought to yell until the liquor breaks
Inside his skull: *The creek was up today.*
*The limb gave way. And Jimmy’s in the dark.*
I held his wrist—I tried. The current pulled
Harder than God, or gravity, or me.
His shoes came off. I saw his small, white face
Turn up toward the sky, then turn away,
Rolling like pulpwood where the bend goes black
Beneath the roots of that old sycamore.

If I go to him now, his heavy hand
Will cuff my ear before I get the words
Past my own teeth. He’ll ask me why I’m soaked,
Why I came back alone without the bucket.
And when I tell him Jimmy isn’t coming,
He’ll call me liar first, and beat me second,
Then sit down in the dirt and kick the dog
Because the river took the one he liked.

So I stay folded in this hollow frame,
Curled near the crankcase where the burdock blooms.
The metal holds the cold long after sun.
A hawk goes lazy over Miller’s field.
The water keeps on running to the lock,
Six miles away, carrying what is left.
And here I am, tucked small behind the chrome,
Too weak to pull my brother from the mud,
Too scared to wake the only man who could.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a tragic, colloquial poem about a boy who finds an old man named Minnegan dying in the river mud, but is terrified to tell the man's brother because he knows he'll be blamed and beaten.
counterfactuals.output:
I seen Old Minnegan down in the silt,
Where the bank gives way and the dark river tilts.
He was stuck to his ribs in that black, heavy clay,
Just a-choking on water and fading away.

His eyes was wide open, all glassy and wild,
And he reached out his hand like a scared little child.
He rattled real wet when he tried for to speak,
And the mud kept a-sucking him down in the creek.

Now, I oughta run fast up the timber-line track,
To fetch his brother Silas to pull the man back.
Silas got mules and a heavy hemp rope,
He’s the only one living could give the man hope.

But Silas is mean as a rusty old nail,
And he’d hit me so hard I’d be bloody and pale.
If I tell him his brother is dyin' down here,
Silas won't listen, he won't shed a tear.

He’ll say that I shoved him, or tripped him, or lied,
He’ll say it’s my fault that Old Minnegan died.
He’d unbuckle his belt with that look in his eye,
And cut me to ribbons before I could cry.
He always needs someone to take up the blame,
And he treats me like dirt 'cause he hates my dad’s name.

So I sat in the weeds where the river-grass grows,
And watched the mud swallow him up to his nose.
I whispered, "I’m sorry," but stayed out of sight,
Just shivering there in the cold of the night.

The bubbles stopped coming a little past four,
And Minnegan’s hat floated off from the shore.
The river went quiet, just lapping the stones,
Hiding the mud where he left his old bones.

I’m walking home slow now, my boots full of lead,
Trying to practice the words in my head.
When Silas comes asking, I’ll swear I don't know—
I’ll swear I was nowhere near where the weeds grow.

Silas won't beat me tonight for the crime,
But I reckon I’m ruined for all of my time.
Cause the sound of that bubblin' down in the mud
Is gonna stay louder than beatings or blood.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a 4-stanza narrative poem involving a child messenger, a wrecked car by a riverbank, atmospheric rain, and characters named Minnegan and Beany?
counterfactuals.output:
The sky bled a heavy and thunderous gray,
While rain lashed the reeds by the swollen black tide.
Young Beany sped onward to finish the day,
With news sealed in plastic and tucked safe inside.

Beside the steep bank where the waters ran wild,
A shattered sedan lay submerged in the mud.
Its headlights flicked out as the shivering child
Approached the crushed frame in the deafening flood.

Old Minnegan stirred through a spiderwebbed pane,
His knuckles all scraped on the wheel of the car.
Small Beany pressed close through the sheet of the rain
To pass him the note he had carried so far.

“The rescue is coming!” the messenger cried,
As Minnegan read by a faint dashboard glow.
With hope reawakened, the old driver sighed,
While Beany turned back through the darkness below.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: A poem about finding someone near a river who drowned or passed out, written as a frightened kid speaking to a heavy drinker, using imagery of daylight beating like a board and a fish flopped on muddy ground.
counterfactuals.output:
Hey, wake up—please, just open your eyes,
Stop looking through the bottom of that glass.
The daylight’s beating like a board out there,
Flat and heavy on the river grass.

It hurts my head just to stand in the sun,
It knocks on my forehead, hard and bright.
I went down by the bend where the current gets slow,
Where the water turns black and shies from the light.

Past the tangled weeds, down low in the silt,
I saw somebody lying by the river’s edge.
He wasn't swimming, he wasn't fishing,
Just stuck in the mud by the cattail hedge.

His clothes were soaked and his face was blue,
His lips pulled back, not making a sound,
Staring up blank at the blinding sky
Like a fish flopped out on the muddy ground.

I don't know if he drowned or just passed out cold,
He didn't twitch when I called out your name.
I touched his boot and it felt like ice,
And the river kept running along just the same.

You smell like the jar on the kitchen shelf,
You’re slurring your words, but you’ve gotta stand!
The sunlight’s hammering down like wood,
And I’m too scared to go pull on his hand.

Put down the bottle and come to the bank,
Don't fall back asleep on the porch floor, please—
There’s a man down there who ain't breathing right,
And the flies are settling on his knees.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
